content: Incisional hernia (IH) is a known complication that can arise following any type of abdominal incision. Its development is influenced by multiple factors and poses a significant burden on both patients and healthcare systems. Over time, incisional hernias tend to enlarge, leading to symptoms such as pain, discomfort, and limitations in daily activities. They can also cause cosmetic concerns, skin-related issues, and, more critically, complications like bowel obstruction, incarceration, and strangulation of the hernia. The majority of abdominal incisional hernias occur due to early wound failure and separation, typically within the first month after surgery. Several perioperative factors are recognized as contributing to wound failure, including surgical site infection, suboptimal closure techniques, wound ischemia, and excessive physical strain, such as from coughing or lifting. Additionally, certain patient-related comorbidities increase the risk of wound failure. These include obesity, malnutrition, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic use of steroids or oral anticoagulants, chronic lung disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and advanced age. The location of the abdominal incision also plays a role in the likelihood of developing an incisional hernia. For example, herniation rates at trocar sites following laparoscopic procedures range from 0.65% to 2.8% in low-risk patients but can increase to as high as 37.1% in high-risk patients with comorbidities such as obesity, diabetes, advanced age, or chronic pulmonary disease. Similarly, the incidence of incisional hernia after midline laparotomy varies from 9% in low-risk patients to 44% in high-risk patients. To prevent the occurrence of incisional hernias, the use of mesh prophylaxis during the closure of abdominal incisions has been proposed. This intervention involves the use of either synthetic or biological meshes. Synthetic meshes, such as those made from polyester or polypropylene, are permanent and provide structural strength by inducing inflammation and promoting ingrowth of the abdominal wall. On the other hand, biological meshes are associated with benefits such as improved biocompatibility, enhanced native tissue integration, better tolerance to infections, and reduced adhesion formation. Surgical mesh is already widely used in hernia repair and is increasingly being employed in abdominal wall reconstructions. However, the use of mesh is not without risks. Potential complications include wound infections, mesh infections, hematomas, seromas, chronic pain, and the formation of a meshoma, which occurs when the mesh wrinkles and causes localized issues. The incidence and cost of mesh explantation have been found to be comparable to the rates of common bile duct injury following cholecystectomy. In the context of hernia recurrence prevention, mesh augmentation has demonstrated superiority over suture repair, with studies showing that mesh repair reduces recurrence rates by half. This benefit is also observed in secondary prevention, such as in open groin hernia repairs, where the risk of recurrence is reduced by 50% to 75% with mesh use. The same principle applies to primary mesh augmentation (PMA), which has been increasingly shown to prevent incisional hernias. Recent meta-analyses have led to the European Hernia Society issuing a weak recommendation for PMA in high-risk patients. Given that one-third of individuals in developed countries will undergo abdominal surgery at some point in their lives, it is crucial to evaluate the current evidence supporting mesh prophylaxis as a strategy to reduce the incidence of incisional hernias. This approach has the potential to improve patient outcomes and alleviate the burden on healthcare systems. As new clinical trials are conducted, further meta-analyses will be essential to better understand the efficacy of PMA in both highand low-risk patient groups and to clarify the potential risks associated with this intervention.
